questions.why: An exclamation never inverts. Que and comme sit in front of an untouched statement: subject, verb, rest. Inversion belongs to questions.

questions.q: Complete with one word: « ___ beau bateau ! » (What a beautiful boat!)
questions.why: Quel takes the noun and agrees with it. The English a is already inside quel, so no article follows it.
Maison is feminine singular, so quelle. Qu'elle is the same sound but a different structure: que + the pronoun elle, which would need a verb after it.

questions.q: Which one needs a verb after it?
questions.why: Qu'elle is que + elle, so a verb follows: Qu'elle est belle ! The quel forms are adjectives and take a noun: Quelle belle voix !

questions.q: Only one of these can be embedded under another verb, as in « Tu sais ___ il est têtu. » Which?
questions.why: Comme keeps its exclamative sense inside a larger sentence. Tu sais que il est têtu would mean you know that he is stubborn, a reported fact rather than an exclamation.
Que de + noun is the quantity exclamation, with no article. Comme cannot do this, and the spoken equivalent is il y a tellement de monde.
Quel replaces the article, it does not sit in front of one. English what a becomes quel on its own.

questions.q: Rewrite as an exclamation with comme: « Elle chante bien. »
questions.why: Nothing moves. Comme is bolted onto the front of the statement, exactly like est-ce que on a question.

questions.q: « Il y a ___ monde ! » (so many people)
questions.why: Si and tellement intensify an adjective (c'est si beau). With a noun the quantity form is tellement de, the same split as aussi against autant de in the comparative.

questions.q: Which of these is a question, not an exclamation?
questions.why: Qu'est-ce que has two lives. A question leaves a gap where the object belongs; an exclamation is already a complete sentence and only adds intensity.

questions.q: Build the exclamation: That boat is so beautiful! (pronoun first, noun at the end)
questions.why: Right dislocation: exclaim with the pronoun, then name the thing after a comma. Very common in speech, and the pronoun and the noun point at the same boat.

questions.q: Build the exclamation: What luck you have!
questions.why: Quel can carry a whole clause behind its noun, still with no inversion: Quelle chance tu as ! and Quel bateau tu as acheté !

questions.q: Rank these from most formal to most casual: 1 Ce que c'est beau ! 2 Que c'est beau ! 3 Qu'est-ce que c'est beau ! 4 Comme c'est beau !
questions.why: Que is the written one, comme the neutral default, ce que casual, qu'est-ce que the heaviest spoken form. All four fill the same slot and mean the same thing.

questions.q: Fix the sentence: « Que c'est très beau ! »
questions.why: Que already does the intensifying, so très is doing the same job twice. Keep one: Que c'est beau ! or C'est très beau !
Quelle and belle both agree with the feminine journée, and the liaison runs quelle into belle into journée as one breath.

questions.q: Give the four ways French exclaims, one example each: a clause, a noun, a quantity, and a plain intensifier.
a: Clause: Comme ce bateau est beau ! (also Que / Ce que / Qu'est-ce que, same slot, different register). Noun: Quel beau bateau ! with quel agreeing and no article. Quantity: Que de monde ! or in speech Il y a tellement de monde ! Intensifier inside a normal sentence: C'est si beau ! / C'est tellement beau ! The rule that ties them together is that none of them invert.
questions.why: Choosing is a matter of what carries the weight: the adjective, the noun, the amount, or nothing in particular.
A fixed exclamation, what a shame. Dommage is masculine, so quel: compare quelle horreur and quelle chance, both feminine.
